title: Pacing Controller Experiment Journal
content:
Status and purpose:

This is a running journal for the pacing-controller experiments: an alternative to the current continuous-batcher heuristics that aims to reduce tail latency without sacrificing throughput for mixed workloads. The idea is to introduce a soft pacing token that modulates batch admission and flush timing based on urgency, observed microbursts, and per-request deadlines.

High-level goals:
- Reduce p95/p99/p999 latency for latency-sensitive tiers (tier A) during microbursts while maintaining overall GPU utilization >= 85%.
- Improve short-request fairness: avoid long, low-urgency requests repeatedly blocking short, high-urgency queries.
- Keep throughput impact < 6% for throughput-oriented workloads.

Motivation / problem statement:
We see recurrent tail spikes when small, urgent requests intermix with a stream of large/long-token requests. Continuous coalescers create large batches that are efficient but increase head-of-line blocking. Existing fairness heuristics (age-weighting + urgency demotion) partly help, but still miss microburst boundaries and produce p999 spikes under realistic client arrival distributions. The pacing controller aims to smooth admission and provide explicit reservation tokens to urgent requests.

Hypotheses to test:
1) Introducing a per-slot pacing budget that refills at a rate proportional to historical arrival intensity will reduce p999 for tier A by > 20% without significant throughput loss.
2) A two-stage flush policy (pacing-triggered flush + timeout flush) reduces unnecessary flushes and improves GPU amortization compared to fixed timeouts.
3) Adding a fairness floor (min-urgency tokens reserved per window) prevents starvation of short queries when long ones dominate.

Experiment design and knobs:
- Knobs implemented in prototype branch: num_slots, pacing_refill_ms, max_wait_ms, urgency_reserve_pct, large_request_demote_threshold, deadline_multiplier.
- Schedules: steady (poisson arrivals at 500 rps), bursty (background steady + periodic microbursts 2000 rps for 200ms), mixed-size (40% short 10-token, 40% medium 64-token, 20% long 512-token).
- Tiers: Tier A (latency-sensitive, per-request soft deadline 100ms), Tier B (best-effort).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99/p999 for latency, tail fairness index (new metric: ratio of short-query p99 to long-query p99), GPU utilization, throughput (tokens/s), average batch size, batch lifetime distribution, number of flushes per second, and cache/KV hit interaction.
- Tracing: request-level traces with entry/queue/flush/first-byte/complete timestamps, plus kernel durations and memcpy times. Profiling with perf maps + flame graphs for top runs.

Benchmark infra and baseline:
- Baseline is current continuous-batcher with dynamic-timeout=8ms and age-weight=1.0. We run all experiments on a single p4d.24xl instance with model v2.6-quant, context=2048. Run IDs recorded below.

Key runs and observations (summary):

Run 2024-10-21-pt1 (bursty mixed-size, pacing disabled baseline)- p95: 63ms, p99: 142ms, p999: 463ms- GPU util: 91%- avg batch size: 28 tokens- Notes: large p999 spikes coincide with microbursts that trigger large batches containing several long requests.

Run 2024-10-23-pt2 (pacing enabled, refill 50 tokens/100ms, max_wait 35ms, reserve 12% for Tier A)- p95: 59ms, p99: 96ms, p999: 236ms (49% reduction vs baseline)- GPU util: 86%- avg batch size: 24 tokens- batch lifetime 90th pct reduced by 18%- Notes: pacing smoothed admission; urgent requests often consumed reserve tokens and bypassed long queues. Some throughput loss for long requests visible but within target.

Run 2024-10-28-pt3 (more aggressive refill 100 tokens/100ms, max_wait 20ms, reserve 6%)- p95: 62ms, p99: 110ms, p999: 310ms- GPU util: 80%- avg batch size: 20 tokens- Notes: too aggressive pacing reduces utilization and increases average latency for long requests; worst-case p999 worse than pt2.

Run 2024-10-30-pt4 (two-stage flush: pacing-trigger flush at 30ms + timeout flush 60ms)- p95: 58ms, p99: 92ms, p999: 210ms- GPU util: 87%- avg batch size: 25 tokens- Notes: two-stage flush reduced unnecessary mid-size flushes and improved both tail metrics and utilization.

Fairness-specific probing (2024-11-01-pt5)- Scenario: adversarial sequence where long requests arrive in steady stream and short urgent arrivals at low rate (10 rps).- Without reserve: short-query p99 >> long-query p99 by factor 6.- With reserve=10%: short-query p99 reduced to parity with long-query p99, overall p999 preserved.

Debug traces and root cause insights:
- Many p999 spikes are due to batch composition: a long request admitted early in a batch extends the kernel time and delays subsequent small requests in the same batch.
- The admission window for continuous coalescing is too permissive under microbursts, producing a small number of huge batches that dominate tail metrics.
- Prefetch/memcpy latency contributed ~8-12ms in runs with large batches; splitting kernels (when possible) and keeping average batch size smaller reduced memcpy overhead fraction.

Metrics to watch and custom metrics added:
- Tail Fairness Index (TFI): p99(short)/p99(long) — ideal ~1.0, bad > 2.0- Pacing Pressure: fraction of requests that had to wait for pacing tokens > 1ms- Batch Skew: stdev(batch_request_sizes)/mean(batch_request_sizes)

Practical knobs and recommended defaults (candidate):
- pacing_refill_ms: 100ms- pacing_refill_tokens: 50- max_wait_ms (pacing-trigger): 30ms- timeout_flush_ms: 60ms- urgency_reserve_pct (tier A): 10%- large_request_demote_threshold: 256 tokens

Tradeoffs observed and guidance:
- Increasing pacing refill reduces tail but harms utilization. There is a convex tradeoff; choose the knee using target SLO and utilization constraints.
- Reserve helps short-query fairness but needs to be budgeted relative to expected short-query volume to avoid starving long requests. Dynamic reserve that scales with short-query arrival rate worked better in pt2 experiments than fixed small reserves.
- Two-stage flush avoids premature flushes during microbursts and reduces wasted kernel startup costs when a burst subsides.

Open questions and follow-ups:
1) Can we learn pacing_refill dynamically from short-term arrival rate estimates instead of a fixed token refill? (next experiment: run an online estimator using EWMA of arrival rate).
2) Interaction with KV/prefix cache: are reserved tokens causing poor KV locality for long-batched requests? Test with a representative cache-miss rate.
3) Multi-tenant behavior: results currently single-tenant; need to repeat in shared cluster with noisy neighbors and background large-batch workloads.
4) Rollout strategy: incremental canary with telemetry for TFI, p999, and GPU util; fallback to baseline policy on regression.

Action items:
- (Riley) Finalize automated EWMA arrival estimator prototype and schedule runs against mixed-size bursty workload. Due 2024-11-10.
- (Maya) Add TFI instrumentation to trace pipeline and dashboard. Due 2024-11-05.
- (Jared) Run multi-tenant replay with recorded production traces from Oct QPS spikes. Due 2024-11-15.
- (SRE) Prepare canary plan: monitor TFI, p999, GPU util; auto rollback threshold p999 > baseline * 1.2. Due 2024-11-20.

Appendix: quick notes on implementation details
- Pacing state is sharded per-worker core to avoid global locking; each shard maintains refill tokens and a small circular buffer of recently admitted request timestamps for local arrival-rate estimation.
- Reservation logic applies at admission-time: if request is Tier A and shard_reserve_tokens>0 admit immediately using reserve token; else follow pacing token path.
- Flush semantics: pacing-trigger flush marks batch for immediate dispatch if pacing budget exhausted or deadline reached; timeout flush remains as a safety net to avoid starvation.

Concluding notes:
Early experiments show the pacing controller is promising: with careful tuning (pt2 configuration) we achieved ~50% reduction in p999 while keeping utilization within acceptable bounds. The next step is automated adaptivity for refill and multi-tenant verification.

Quick links to artifacts and traces (for reviewers):
- perf trace bundle pt2: https://perf.redwood/team/traces/run-20241023-pt2- flame graph: https://perf.redwood/team/flames/run-20241023-pt2/flame.html- PR with prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987

Notes to self:
- When we run the EWMA experiment, capture not just p999 but the spectrum of batch lifetimes and the number of cross-priority demotions.

End of journal entry.
